name: West Ridge

pitch_detail.notes: An exposed step out over the gully on the left, then a right-trending chimney feature up to trees; one easy 5.6 move off the ground, then low 5th to the tree belay.
An exposed rightward ramp, then back left toward unlikely-looking roofs described as the route's physical crux; belay on a ledge just above.
A short wall (watch for a stuck cam at the top) leads through dirty tree ledges and steps to a belay at the base of a hanging slab.
Float up the slab, over a bush/tree, then right and up through steeper, exposed moves with an interesting layback midway.
The last technical climbing before the party coils the rope for the scramble across the false summit to the true summit.

rappel_detail.notes: The one rappel most parties make: a 60 m rope doubled clears the step. Two more short slung stations sit at steeper steps lower on the ridge; parties use them on loose or wet rock, or downclimb those steps at Class 3-4.
rappel_detail.anchor: tree or rock horn with webbing and rap rings (climber-maintained, not bolted)
hazards: Climber-maintained tat: inspect it and back it up or replace it.
Loose, dirty rock around the second step; keep the party close, the ridge is exposed on both sides.
rappel_detail.station: The first fixed anchor, at the steepest, most exposed step just below the summit block on the East Ridge (the short Class 4 crux).

rappels: Descend the East Ridge: one rappel from the first tree anchor over the steepest step below the summit block, then scrambling; up to two more optional short rappels from slung stations lower down
descent_text: From the true summit, the standard descent follows the East Ridge back toward Bumblebee Pass rather than reversing the West Ridge climb. Walk/scramble off the east end of the summit block on a faint climbers' path to a notch where several parties over the years have left fixed tree anchors (webbing and rap rings, not bolts) at three points along the ridge's steeper steps — roughly around 6,200 ft and lower. Descent style varies by party and conditions: some downclimb the entire East Ridge unroped (sustained, exposed class 3–4 with a couple of low-5th moves), while most rope up for at least one section. A common approach is a single double-rope rappel (60m rope, doubled) off the initial tree anchor to bypass the steepest, most exposed step, then class 3 scrambling the rest of the way down; other parties describe using two to three shorter rappels off successive tree stations (doubled 8mm/thin rope, ~30m per rap) where the rock is loose or holds are wet, downclimbing the easier sections between them. Inspect any tat/rap rings before weighting them and back them up or replace old webbing if in doubt — these are climber-maintained natural anchors, not resupplied by any agency. Once off the ridge's technical ground, descend talus back into Bumblebee Basin, regain the steep boot path up and over Bumblebee Pass, drop back to the PCT near Ridge Lake, and retrace the Kendall Katwalk and switchbacks south to the PCT North Trailhead.
approach: Park at the PCT North (Commonwealth Basin) Trailhead lot just off the frontage road at Exit 52, Snoqualmie Pass (~3,000 ft) — cross under I-90, take the first right, and the lot is on the right. From the trailhead, follow the Pacific Crest Trail northbound; it climbs steadily through timber via long switchbacks for roughly 5.5–6 miles to the Kendall Katwalk (~5,400 ft), a narrow, exposed ledge blasted directly into a granite cliff on the ridge north of Kendall Peak — solid underfoot but very exposed, use caution if icy or in high wind. Continue north on the PCT about a mile past the Katwalk, dropping slightly, to Ridge Lake (~5,260 ft), the last reliable water source and a common camp/rest stop (roughly 2–2.5 hrs / ~7 mi in from the car). About 0.4–0.5 mile past Ridge Lake, watch for an unsigned but obvious climbers' boot path branching left (west) off the PCT; it climbs a steep ~200 ft to Bumblebee Pass (~5,400 ft), a small saddle above Alaska Lake. The path is loose and eroded in spots on both the up and down sides — take care with footing. Drop off the far side of the pass into Bumblebee Basin (scattered camps, seasonal water), then contour/ascend northwest across talus and scree (worse-looking than it climbs) toward the lowest notch on Thomson's west ridgeline (~5,960 ft). Short sections of 4th-class scrambling around a set of gendarmes lead to the notch at the base of the route, where the first pitch starts just left (north) of the crest. Total trailhead-to-base distance is about 8–8.5 miles with roughly 2,900–3,000 ft of gain, typically 4–5 hours for a fit party; most groups do the climb car-to-car in one long day, though the basin makes a fine camp for a two-day trip.
overview: Mount Thomson (6,554 ft; spelled 'Thompson' in most published descriptions, 'Thomson' on USGS/Green Trails maps) is a sharp, Matterhorn-like andesite peak on the PCT divide roughly 4 miles northeast of Snoqualmie Pass, in the Alpine Lakes Wilderness (Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Snoqualmie Ranger District). The West Ridge is its classic technical line: sound, porphyritic-andesite rock, rated Grade II, 5.6, with a long wilderness approach that keeps it quieter than roadside Cascades crags.
beta: The West Ridge is Mount Thomson's most technical and aesthetic alpine climbing objective. The route ascends 4-5 pitches of low to mid-fifth-class rock on the west ridge crest, with the crux being a well-featured chimney on pitch 1 and a 5.6 bulge pull on pitch 2. Route-finding is generally straightforward once established on the ridge proper. Multiple belay options exist on comfortable ledges with solid natural anchors. The descent via the East Ridge (Class 3-4) balances the upclimb and includes one optional 20-foot Class 4 rappel.
gear: Light alpine rack: nuts plus cams to about 3 in
Extra slings/runners for rappel anchors and protection
Sturdy approach shoes; rock shoes optional given the moderate grade
